intro: Five long reads: why the public keeps choosing buildings that look old, the 2014 idea that powers today's chatbots, how insurgent parties survive their defeats, the malaria parasite caught mid-break-in, and what weight-loss drugs reveal about gluttony and desire.

stories.headline: Most people want buildings that look old
stories.dek: Thirty years of polling find large, stable majorities for traditional architecture, which makes the profession's near-total devotion to modernism a puzzle.
body: Taste in buildings is usually treated as a matter beyond argument. Robert Kwolek, a senior architectural designer at the British group Create Streets, writing in Works in Progress, thinks that is wrong on the evidence. Whatever one thinks of individual buildings, he argues, the public's preferences between architectural styles are not scattered and idiosyncratic. They are remarkably consistent, and they point overwhelmingly one way.

The background is the long reign of modernism. The style emerged in the 1920s, stripping away ornament, exposing steel and concrete, and abandoning the intricate patterns of traditional facades and street plans. By the 1950s it dominated building across the world, and styles of broadly modernist character still do. Kwolek's question is simple: do the people who live with these buildings actually like them?

Critics on opposite sides have long agreed that they do not. John Summerson, the English architectural historian, was sympathetic to modernism, yet in 1940 he wrote that the public could not understand it and hated it intensely. Wolf von Eckardt, a German-American critic who disliked the style, declared it dead in 1977 and remarked that nobody mourned, because it had never been popular. Kwolek's point is that a friend and an enemy made the same observation.
## From town meetings to polling firms

The tool for testing such claims is the visual preference survey, which shows respondents pairs of images and asks which they prefer. The modern tradition began in Metuchen, New Jersey, in 1979, when the town asked the Rutgers University Urban Design Studio to photograph local streets and have residents rate them at a public meeting. Residents favoured detailed, varied, human-scale streetscapes and disliked blank buildings and wide, car-dominated roads; the town later wrote a design code on the results. Kwolek is candid that meeting attendees are not a representative sample, and that the images were not controlled closely enough to show which features drove the answers.

Britain took up the method in the late 1980s. In 1987 David Halpern, then a Cambridge undergraduate and later a prominent behavioural scientist, showed students twelve faces and twelve buildings. They agreed about the faces, but architecture students' preferences among the buildings often sharply contradicted everyone else's. Similar studies in Canada in 2001, Britain in 2015 and Chile in 2019 found the same gap between professional and lay judgement.

The first properly sampled survey came in 1998, when the British Market Research Bureau polled for the Popular Housing Forum using sets of new-build house styles. Ninety-four per cent of potential buyers preferred the more traditional options, and 92 per cent of other respondents wanted a traditional option built near them. Kwolek counts around twenty properly sampled surveys since the 1990s, mostly British, with others in America, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal and Chile. In every one, more than 60 per cent favoured traditional architecture; in many, more than 85 per cent did.

Among the early studies he rates most highly is one commissioned in 2009 by ADAM Architecture, which showed four real commercial buildings in matching perspectives and weather. Both modernist examples had won prizes; 77 per cent still preferred the traditional pair. In Évora, Portugal, Luis Balula found in 2008–09 that experts and laypeople both rated old buildings highly but parted ways on new ones, with non-experts liking a pastiche Mediterranean housing scheme that experts disliked, and the reverse for a modernist block.
## Better pictures, same answer

The weakness of the older work was control: if the modern building in a pair is also shown on a grey day or a busier street, the comparison is muddied. Kwolek argues that the past five years have largely fixed this. Image editing, especially with artificial intelligence, has made tightly matched comparisons cheap, and renewed public argument has produced more surveys.

In 2020 the National Civic Art Society asked Americans about seven pairs of real federal buildings and courthouses, matched as far as possible for massing and context. Traditional designs averaged 72 per cent. Partisanship barely mattered: 70 per cent of Democrats and 73 per cent of Republicans agreed. Women were keener than men (77 against 67 per cent), and over-65s keener than 18–34-year-olds (77 against 68).

Create Streets has since run a string of British polls holding context and rendering constant. A classical alternative for a rugby stadium in Bath beat the utilitarian original by 74 to 26, and even 18–24-year-olds preferred it, 61 to 39. Brick-clad viaducts for the HS2 railway beat bare concrete by 69 to 28. A Gothic counter-proposal for a new library at Christ's College, Cambridge, of the same floor area as Grafton Architects' design, won 71 to 21 among more than 2,000 adults. A plan by the architect Francis Terry to keep and extend the facade of a 1920s Marks and Spencer building on Oxford Street beat demolition 79 to 17 among 3,130 adults; even Londoners backed it 72 to 26.

The most striking use of the new tools came from The Aesthetic City in the Netherlands in 2025. In all but one of eight pairs, researchers began with a photograph of a real modernist building and used AI to generate a traditional alternative on the same site, in the same weather, with the same bulk. Traditional versions won between 67 and 92 per cent, averaging 82. An appendix notes a 2026 academic paper finding the same pattern in Norway and Greece, somewhat stronger among Greeks.
## How far the evidence goes

Kwolek takes the obvious objections seriously. Sceptics say the public is merely rejecting weak modernist buildings, and that a better one might win. Many surveys, his own organisation's included, were commissioned by groups sympathetic to tradition. His reply is that every pair tested so far has produced the same result. But he concedes that only about three dozen fully controlled pairs have been polled, in just three countries, and he expects firmer conclusions only within a decade. His provisional estimate is that 70 to 90 per cent of people clearly prefer traditional architecture, with only small tilts towards modernism among men, the young and perhaps the wealthier.
## The real puzzle

That leaves the question Kwolek finds most interesting. Nearly all architecture schools teach broadly modernist styles, and perhaps more than 99 per cent of architects practise only in them. In Britain there have been almost no public commissions in traditional styles since the 1950s, private housing being the main exception. Anti-traditional planning rules explain some of this, but the pattern persists where development control is stylistically neutral. Societies keep commissioning buildings their members say they dislike: a gap between stated and revealed preference. He notes that several explanations exist, but leaves testing them for later work.
stories.counterpoint: Kwolek works for Create Streets, which commissioned several of the surveys he cites, and the counter-designs were drawn by people who wanted them to win. Showing a single image of a facade also measures first impressions, not how buildings serve the people who use them for decades, and the gap between what people say and what clients commission may simply reflect costs, programmes and constraints a poll leaves out.
stories.why: If the preference is as broad and stable as these surveys suggest, then the ugliness of new building is not a matter of taste but a failure of the system that commissions it, and a hidden cause of opposition to housing. It turns an aesthetic quarrel into a question of institutions and incentives, which is something policy can change.
questions: If seven in ten people prefer traditional designs, whose preferences is a typical public commission actually serving?
What would a well-designed survey need to show before you would accept that the public genuinely dislikes modernism, rather than bad modernism?
Which explanation for the gap between stated and revealed preference seems most plausible to you: cost, professional training, planning rules or something else?

stories.headline: The intern's glance that built the chatbots
stories.dek: A 2014 fix for machine translation became the engine of modern AI; whether it is also the essence of intelligence is a separate question.
body: Most technological revolutions have tangled origins. Natalie Wolchover, in a column for Quanta Magazine, argues that the current boom in artificial intelligence can be traced with unusual precision to one mathematical idea, devised in 2014 by an intern who did not much believe in the field he was working in.

The intern was Dzmitry Bahdanau, a 23-year-old from Belarus who had done competitive programming but had no research experience. He had joined a lab at the University of Montreal led by Yoshua Bengio, where he worked with a postdoctoral researcher, Kyunghyun Cho. Their project was to get a computer to translate English into French. Bahdanau privately doubted that neural networks could ever reach human-level intelligence. Bengio and Cho believed in them, and saw translation as a hard and worthwhile test.

The idea that came out of that project, which the three called attention, now sits at the heart of systems such as ChatGPT and Claude. Wolchover's column tells how it works, and then asks a bigger question: is the thing it does, in some sense, what intelligence is?
## The bottleneck

Translation resists rules. Grammar, idiom and connotation differ between languages, so swapping words one for one fails. Neural networks, which learn from examples rather than from rules, looked promising because they could be trained on large collections of paired English and French sentences. But their results were mediocre, and they got worse as sentences got longer.

Wolchover locates the cause in the architecture. The networks of the time had an encoder, which read the source sentence, and a decoder, which wrote the translation. The encoder had to squeeze everything in the sentence into a fixed-size memory before the decoder began. A short sentence fitted; a long one overwhelmed the space. More training would not help, because the limit was in the design.
## Looking back as you write

Bahdanau's change was to let the network look back. He gave it a mathematical operation that, while producing each word of the output, could consult the whole of the source sentence rather than a compressed summary of it. He has described the idea as obvious in hindsight, and says it worked the first time. Long sentences were now translated about as well as short ones, which meant the approach could scale, and other researchers adopted it quickly. Bahdanau traces it to his own schooldays, when translating by hand meant glancing back and forth between the text and his draft; he had, he says, turned that habit into a neural mechanism.

Wolchover illustrates what the mechanism must achieve with a pair of sentences. In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', the word 'it' means the animal, which is masculine in French and so becomes il. In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too wide', 'it' means the street, which is feminine and becomes elle. The same English word needs different French words, and only context decides which.
## Queries, keys and values

In the version used today, each word is first turned into a vector, a list of numbers that Wolchover likens to an arrow pointing in some direction. These vectors pass through many layers of connected nodes, whose weights are set in training. Within those layers, each word's vector is converted into three new ones: a query, representing what the word is looking for; a key, representing what it offers to others; and a value, the information it contributes.

Several attention heads then work in parallel. Each compares one word's query with every other word's key, and where the two align closely, that other word's value contributes more to the first word's updated representation. Context is thereby turned into arithmetic. In the encoder, the query for 'it' might amount to a request for an earlier noun that could plausibly be tired; the key for 'animal' fits that request better than the key for 'street', so the animal's information flows into the representation of 'it'. Layer after layer repeats the process, building associations on associations. The decoder, writing the French one word at a time, uses attention to look back at the encoder's work, and so produces il.

None of these associations is programmed. A network begins with random weights and produces nonsense; each error sends a correction backward that nudges the weights. After a vast number of nudges it can translate sentences it has never seen, having learned for itself, in effect, that animals get tired. Experts find individual attention heads hard to interpret, Wolchover notes, though together they capture relationships of many kinds.
## From translation to everything

In 2017 a team at Google published 'Attention Is All You Need', introducing the transformer, which strengthened attention and discarded much of the surrounding machinery. It achieved state-of-the-art translation for a fraction of the training computation of earlier systems, and the paper has since been cited more than 250,000 times. Large language models followed.

The step from translation to chatbots is shorter than it looks. Predicting the next word of a French translation is a special case of predicting the next word of any text. Language models are trained on vast amounts of it, adjusting their connections so that their attention patterns become more useful for that task. Llion Jones, one of the transformer paper's authors and now chief technology officer of Sakana AI, calls the progression a considerable leap. He and others suspect that next-word prediction is 'AI-complete': because predicting text requires translation, arithmetic, mathematics and knowledge of the world, solving it would arguably mean solving AI in general. Language modelling may be the nearest thing we have to a working definition of intelligence.
## The limits of the analogy

Wolchover is careful about what this does and does not show. It may not be accurate to say that a model knows or understands anything in the human sense. For advanced mathematics, frontier systems often lean on formal reasoning and proof-checking tools layered on top of language modelling. And Jones himself no longer thinks attention is all that is needed.

There is also the question of whether human thinking works this way. Recent research cited by Wolchover suggests that it is not purely linguistic: when people think, brain regions beyond the language networks of the cortex become active, drawing on sensory impressions, physical and social experience, memory and reasoning. On this view language is a powerful part of cognition and our way of communicating about the world, not its source. Most animal intelligence, after all, involves no language at all. Nobody yet knows how a human resolves a pronoun like 'it'.

Then there is efficiency. People converse fluently without reading the internet once, and without the energy budget of a data centre. Jones believes the present paradigm will not close that gap and that something quite different will be needed. Wolchover concludes that it makes sense, in hindsight, that solving translation opened the door: translating well implies a kind of understanding, in a person or a machine. Whether attention is the essence of intelligence, or one important part of it, remains open.
stories.counterpoint: The tidy origin story flatters a single idea. Attention mechanisms had relatives in earlier work, and the leap to today's systems owed at least as much to vast data, cheap computation and engineering at scale as to Bahdanau's insight. Calling next-word prediction 'AI-complete' also risks circularity: it defines intelligence as whatever text prediction ends up requiring.
stories.why: Attention is the one mechanism most worth understanding if you want to know what language models are doing when they appear to reason. Wolchover's explanation is clear enough to make that concrete, and her caveats about the brain and efficiency mark out where today's approach may run out.
questions: Does the ability to resolve 'it' correctly count as understanding, or only as a very good imitation of it?
If human thought draws on far more than language, what would an AI need beyond next-word prediction?
Why might it matter, scientifically or ethically, that people learn language so much more efficiently than machines?

stories.headline: Why insurgent parties must first learn to lose
stories.dek: Outsider movements rarely time the collapse of the old order, argues Ben Landau-Taylor; the ones that win have spent years in the wilderness getting ready for it.
body: On the day of Brazil's presidential election, Ben Landau-Taylor sat down with Renan Santos, the candidate of the Mission Party. Running an outsider campaign, Santos told him, means being willing to lose, and lose, and lose, and win. After twelve years of work the party had hoped for a strong showing and gains in the legislature. It got neither. Santos came fourth, with about 2.6m votes, or 2.2% of the total, and the party held its single federal seat without adding another.

Landau-Taylor, writing in Palladium, calls the result thoroughly mediocre. But his essay is not an obituary. He argues that the Mission Party is doing exactly what successful insurgents have always done, and that its defeat is a normal stage in a long process rather than a verdict on it.

The party grew, by Santos's account, out of the mass protests against corruption under President Dilma Rousseff, led by the Free Brazil Movement. When the protests achieved their first aims, the organisers saw no reason to disband, since the country's problems remained. By trial and error they turned the movement's energy and talent into a permanent organisation. Landau-Taylor points to the continued energy at its public events as a sign that it is not giving up.
## The common arc

The general pattern, as he describes it, has two phases. First comes a long period in the wilderness, shut out of respectable politics, during which an insurgent party builds internal infrastructure: members, trained operatives, a settled doctrine and the ability to mobilise people. Then a major part of the mainstream collapses. The party that has done the groundwork moves quickly to fill the vacuum, because its organisers, its ideology and its capacity to put people on the streets already exist. Most insurgent parties fail. Those that succeed, he argues, tend to fit this shape.
## Bolsheviks and Free Soilers

His first case is Russia. The first Russian Marxist organisation was founded in 1883. Through the 1890s its factions built networks through newspapers, party conferences, arrests, prison and exile. In the revolution of 1905, which produced a short-lived constitutional monarchy, they played a minor part; Lenin later called it a dress rehearsal. When the exhausted Tsarist regime gave way in 1917 under the strain of the first world war, the Bolsheviks moved quickly to lead the rioters and mutineers, and from there fought the civil war that gave them total power.

His second is the American anti-slavery movement. The Liberty Party, the country's first anti-slavery party, was founded in 1841. In 1848 much of it merged into the Free Soil Party, which won a handful of congressional seats by opposing the spread of slavery into the western territories. Then in 1854 the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which opened the way for slavery's westward expansion, split the Whigs, one of the two major parties, and shattered their tired coalition. As the Republican Party formed from the wreckage, the Free Soilers merged into it, bringing future leading figures such as Salmon P. Chase and Charles Sumner.

He adds a list of briefer examples: the Young Turks as the Ottoman sultanate declined, the Labour Party filling the space left by the sudden collapse of Britain's Liberals, the Nazis rising as the Weimar government disintegrated, and Charles de Gaulle's Fifth Republic replacing the Fourth.
## Two American parties

Landau-Taylor then turns to the present, and here his account is openly partisan in tone. The Democratic Socialists of America were founded in the 1980s, but he dates their current form to 2016, when Bernie Sanders's campaign popularised democratic socialism and the group reorganised around his supporters. By 2017 it had loosened its chapter rules, quintupled its membership and left the Socialist International; in 2018 it sent its first members to Congress. He describes it as an insurgent caucus inside the Democratic Party, steadily improving its organising, doctrine and turnout operations.

The mainstream party first dismissed it as disreputable. In Landau-Taylor's telling, the party's liberal ideology then decayed: he treats 2020 as a turning point and argues that the party machine lost its internal legitimacy in 2024, when it backed Joe Biden and then replaced him with Kamala Harris. Since then, he says, mainstream Democrats have adopted much of the DSA's platform, and Zohran Mamdani's election as mayor of New York, defeating Andrew Cuomo and Eric Adams, is the movement's signature success.

The right, he argues, shows what happens when no cadre is waiting. The conservative Republican establishment lost its ideological confidence after Barack Obama's presidency and abandoned its pretences in the 2016 primary. There was no organised insurgent faction ready to take over; the existing right-wing groups were subordinate to the conservative coalition and had built no ideology that could justify ruling. So the vacuum was filled by Donald Trump personally. His first term, Landau-Taylor argues, was largely ineffective for lack of trained people. By the second, the coalition had achieved enough order to pursue bureaucratic goals more effectively, but it still lacks the personal and ideological cohesion of the earlier cases.
## Timing belongs to individuals

The strategic lesson follows. Collapses can sometimes be foreseen in outline but never timed, because the details depend so heavily on particular people. Had Biden's health held for a few more years, had H. H. Asquith and David Lloyd George avoided splitting the Liberals, or had Franklin Pierce not backed the Kansas-Nebraska Act, each collapse might have come years later. When it does come, the vacuum goes to whoever combines the best existing infrastructure, skill at political manoeuvre and a willingness to take critical risks. That might be Lenin's organised vanguard, he writes, or a New York property dealer with no plan or ideology who finds the field open.
## Brazil, again

The essay ends where it began. Landau-Taylor concedes that no one can say when, or whether, the Mission Party's opening will come, and his historical cases are illustrations rather than proof of a law. But he thinks the structure of the moment is suggestive. Brazil's run-off pits Lula, the 80-year-old incumbent who has served time in prison, against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president, who is under house arrest and barred from standing for office himself. Neither is widely liked, but both party machines still work well enough to run an election. If they stop working, Landau-Taylor concludes, the opening will go to whoever is ready. The Mission Party's job is to keep building cadre, doctrine and the means of mobilisation, and to keep losing until it does not.
stories.counterpoint: The argument is built from survivors. For every Bolshevik or Free Soil party that waited and won, many organisations built cadre for decades and never got their moment, so preparation looks necessary only because failures go unrecorded. The essay's account of recent American politics is also contestable on its own terms: much of what it calls collapse could be read as ordinary coalition bargaining.
stories.why: It offers a useful corrective to the habit of judging movements by their latest vote share. For anyone trying to change an institution from outside, a party, a profession or a church, the essay's claim is that the decisive work is unglamorous capacity-building done long before an opening appears.
questions: How would you tell the difference between a movement in its wilderness years and one that is simply failing?
Is it a strength or a danger that the vacuum goes to whoever is ready, whatever their ideas?
Which institutions you know well would be filled by a prepared outsider if their leadership suddenly lost legitimacy?

source.title: Lose, and Lose, and Lose, and Win
source.author: Ben Landau-Taylor

stories.headline: How the malaria parasite picks the lock
stories.dek: Cryo-electron microscopy has caught Plasmodium forcing its way into a red blood cell, revealing a molecular wedge that may offer a new way to stop it.
body: Malaria has been one of humanity's great killers for most of recorded history. Medieval Italians blamed it on the bad air of swamps, which gave the disease its name. In the 20th century it caused up to 5% of all deaths worldwide, and the World Health Organization still estimates that it kills about 600,000 people a year.

Joanna Thompson, writing in Quanta Magazine, reports on a study that has, for the first time, watched in molecular detail the moment the parasite breaks into the cells it feeds on. The work, led by Chi-Min Ho, a microbiologist and structural biologist at Columbia University, and published in Cell, answers a question that has resisted scientists for half a century, and suggests a new kind of drug.
## A long hunt

The cause of malaria was unknown until about 150 years ago. In 1880 Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran, a French physician, looked at a soldier's blood through a simple microscope and saw a single-celled organism, a protist of the genus Plasmodium. Since then researchers have mapped its life cycle, its hosts and the differences between species, which cause somewhat different forms of the disease.

That cycle is intricate. The parasite reproduces sexually in a mosquito's gut; humans serve as a reservoir where it waits to be picked up by another insect. Inside a person it changes shape and size from stage to stage, at times egg-like, thread-like or star-shaped. Some stages move fast; the hypnozoite, which lodges in the liver, can lie dormant for years. When it reaches the small, round merozoite stage, it is ready to invade red blood cells, which Thompson describes as its food supply.

How it gets in has been studied with ever better tools. In the 1970s, electron microscopy showed a thickening of the membrane where parasite met cell, and the parasite seemed to merge with the cell rather like a droplet joining a pool. A 1978 film from James Dvorak's laboratory at America's National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, one of the first of its kind, caught parasites entering a red cell. But the proteins responsible could not be isolated for decades.

Earlier work did establish the outline. The parasite inserts a ring of protein anchors into the host's membrane, known collectively as the moving junction. It grips these anchors with its own surface proteins and pushes forward through a temporary portal, and the membrane seals behind it. The whole manoeuvre takes less than a minute. What nobody understood was how the portal itself worked.
## The wedge

Ho's group used cryo-electron microscopy, which images samples frozen in a near-natural state, to capture the moving junction at the moment of invasion in unprecedented detail. They examined the four protein units in each anchor. Three, they found, form a dense wedge beneath the surface of the membrane; the fourth links that wedge to the invading parasite.

Many such anchors are placed on the cell's surface, and their electrical properties generate forces that push aside the lipid molecules of which the membrane is made. This reverses the membrane's curvature, so that it bows inward around the parasite. Some of the displaced lipids reassemble into a protective envelope around the invader before the cell's membrane re-forms and seals. What the microscopists of the 1970s saw as something like a droplet merging with a pool turns out to be a mechanical operation: the parasite physically reshapes the membrane it is passing through. Jake Baum, a parasitologist at the University of New South Wales who was not involved, called the paper mind-blowing, and described it as biophysics more than molecular biology, the product of a field that had built step by step towards a powerful observation.
## Life inside

Once in, the parasite remodels its new home. Red cells have no nucleus or organelles, so it builds what it needs from scratch; Ho compares this to turning an empty warehouse into a loft flat. It also changes the cell's surface, displaying adhesive proteins that make infected cells stick to blood-vessel walls, a cause of severe symptoms. Kirk Deitsch of Weill Cornell Medicine reported in 2025 that the parasite switches between these proteins over days or weeks, helping it evade the immune system and the spleen. It then takes on a flexible, amoeba-like form that further helps it escape clearance, and replicates for about 48 hours until the cell bursts. The released parasites invade fresh cells, and within days millions may be circulating.
## A narrow window

Treatment has been a running battle. Older drugs such as chloroquine, sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine attack the parasite in the bloodstream, and Plasmodium is rapidly evolving resistance to them. Without a detailed picture of invasion, Deitsch says, much drug research was done essentially blind, by trial and error.

Ho's argument is that blocking entry would stop the parasite before it establishes an infection. Her team used an AI-powered protein-design platform to create a protein that targets the moving junction, and in test tubes it prevented parasites from entering red cells. It has not yet been tested for safety or effectiveness in animals.

There are reasons for caution. Van Ooij, a molecular parasitologist at Keele University, points out that because invasion takes only about a minute, a drug would have a narrow window: it would need to stay stable in the body for a long time, act very fast, or both. Some researchers have long argued that invasion is a poor drug target for exactly this reason.
## Beyond malaria

The findings may travel. Plasmodium belongs to the apicomplexans, a large group of parasitic protists that includes Toxoplasma gondii, carried by cats, and Cyclospora, which causes severe diarrhoea. These relatives appear to use similar invasion machinery, so a better understanding of malaria's could help against toxoplasmosis and cyclosporiasis too. A separate 2026 paper described how Toxoplasma senses the right moment to deploy its moving junction, and malaria may work in the same way.

Ho's laboratory now plans to apply the same methods to other protein complexes involved in infection, including the adhesive proteins that keep infected cells away from the spleen. Having caught one white whale, as she puts it, the team wants to go after the rest. (Thompson notes that the research was partly funded by the Simons Foundation, which also funds Quanta, and that this did not influence the coverage.)
stories.counterpoint: A structure is not a drug. The inhibitor has worked only in test tubes, and a protein therapy that must act within a minute-long window, in a parasite that evolves resistance quickly, faces formidable obstacles in dosing, stability and cost for the poor countries that carry most of malaria's burden. Cheaper, proven tools such as bed nets and the new vaccines may matter far more in the near term.
stories.why: It shows how far structural biology has come: a process glimpsed as a blur in 1978 can now be described molecule by molecule. It also illustrates a broader shift in drug discovery, from trial and error towards rational design guided by precise structures and AI-designed proteins.
questions: Why might seeing a mechanism clearly be worth more than decades of trial-and-error screening?
If invasion lasts only a minute, what properties would a successful drug need, and are they realistic?
How should funders weigh basic structural research against proven interventions when lives are at stake now?

source.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
source.author: Joanna Thompson

stories.headline: When a drug quiets appetite, what becomes of gluttony?
stories.dek: Amy Mantravadi argues that GLP-1 drugs expose gluttony as a disorder of desire, and that Christians may take them or not but are never free to stop desiring God.
body: The Gila monster eats only once or twice a year, a habit that drew scientists' interest in the 1980s. In 1992 researchers isolated a compound from its venom, exendin-4, which resembled GLP-1, a hormone that had helped diabetic mice, but lasted longer in the body. By the 2010s drugs that mimic GLP-1 were treating diabetes effectively, and producing striking weight loss as a side-effect. Amy Mantravadi, writing in Mere Orthodoxy, notes Gallup polling that suggests America's obesity rate peaked in 2022 and has since fallen. Drugs have done what years of advice about diet and exercise did not.

Her question is theological: what does this do to the Christian understanding of gluttony? Her answer is that the drugs expose something the church had half forgotten. Gluttony, she argues, was never chiefly about food. It is a disorder of desire, and desire is what these medicines touch.
## A sin Scripture barely names

Mantravadi begins by admitting how little the Bible says directly. Proverbs 23:20 warns against keeping company with heavy drinkers and gluttonous eaters; Deuteronomy 21:20 describes a rebellious son as a glutton and a drunkard. No verse plainly forbids gluttony. It has to be inferred from commands against covetousness and hoarding and preoccupation with worldly things, or read as a failure to care for one's body or neighbour. It appears in neither the Ten Commandments nor the Sermon on the Mount, yet the early church counted it among the capital vices, perhaps shaped by Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where the virtue of temperance implies an opposing vice. Even its scope is debatable: does it concern only food and drink? Can it include eating too little? Is it a sin against others or oneself?
## What the tradition saw

The tradition, she shows, was more subtle than the modern picture. Augustine, in book ten of the Confessions, distinguishes the body's need for nourishment from the sinful pleasure that rides along with it, and confesses that it is hard to tell which is which. He leaves particular rules of diet to conscience, following Paul's teaching on disputable matters.

Gregory the Great, in the Moralia, warns that sins of the flesh weaken a person for spiritual battle, and names five forms of gluttony: eating too early, seeking luxurious food, fussing over its preparation, eating too much, and surrendering wholly to the craving for it. Mantravadi observes that modern Christians think of gluttony almost entirely in terms of the fourth.

Thomas Aquinas supplies the decisive language of disorder. Gluttony is not any desire to eat but an inordinate one, a desire that departs from reason and so from virtue. Eating a great deal is not in itself the sin; the sin lies in pursuing the pleasures of the palate for their own sake. Aquinas keeps Gregory's categories of quality, quantity, timing and manner.

Later shifts dulled the concept. Where food was scarce, overeating was a sign of greed and even oppression; in an age of plenty it came to look like a mere lapse in self-control. Protestant insistence on enjoying God's gifts, a reaction against medieval asceticism, led many to stop talking about gluttony at all. Some Christians now stretch the term to doomscrolling, and eating disorders have been described as disordered desire, but the popular image remains an overweight person eating junk.
## What the drugs reveal

That image, Mantravadi notes, carried an old assumption that thinness signals godliness. In the 2010s attitudes softened, as research stressed genetics, environment and additives and critics attacked body-shaming. The arrival of Ozempic and Wegovy has reversed some of that: rapid weight loss is now treated as suspicious, a kind of cheating.

The drugs do not burn fat. They act on the brain's reward circuitry and reduce the desire to eat. Mantravadi draws on the work of Kent Berridge, a neuroscientist at the University of Michigan, whose research from the 1980s suggested that wanting something is neurologically distinct from liking it: one is the urge to pursue a reward, the other the pleasure of receiving it. A Kaiser Family Foundation survey found that one in eight American adults is taking a GLP-1 drug, which she calls one of the largest health experiments ever run on the public.

The experiment has unsettling reports. The New York Times described users who felt emotionally flatter, less connected to the social side of eating, duller or more lethargic; Marie Spreckley, a Cambridge researcher, said such accounts warrant study. Ezra Klein described walking past sweets without craving them, but finding that the loss of desire left him low and anhedonic. Here the old categories wobble. Aquinas warned against too much desire; these drugs can suppress desire as such, and perhaps not only for food. Should a drug-induced loss of appetite be treated differently from a natural one? The church, she says, has barely begun to ask.
## Desire rightly ordered

Her constructive argument rests on Scripture's fuller treatment of desire. Desire is not evil; it is bound up with the will, created good, bent by the Fall and renewed by the Spirit. In Numbers 11 the Israelites, fed with manna, crave meat and remember the food of Egypt; Psalm 78 calls this rebellion, testing God by demanding food to suit their craving. This, for Mantravadi, is Augustine's distinction in action: they had what their bodies needed but wanted pleasure instead. Yet Deuteronomy 12:20 permits them to eat meat whenever they desire it in the land. The fault was not appetite but appetite set against God's word and their own good, a preference for Egypt's luxuries over life under the King who provides. Psalm 145:15–16 shows the proper pattern: God gives food in due season and satisfies the desire of every living thing.

With Aquinas she reads anorexia, bulimia, binge eating and the free-spending foodie alike as forms of bondage to disordered appetite, seeking comfort where it cannot be found, while stressing that these conditions have many causes and that she condemns no one who suffers them. Psalm 37:4 and Proverbs 11:23 point the other way: the desire of the righteous is good because it is ordered towards God. Psalm 73's 'there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you' and C. S. Lewis's The Weight of Glory, which says our desires are not too strong but too weak, like a child content with mud pies who cannot imagine a holiday at the sea, complete the picture.
## The conclusion

Desire, Mantravadi adds, is more than feeling: a father who loves his son may not feel like rising at night to care for him, and what we truly want is shown by how we spend our time and what we worship. Purifying desire cannot be done by self-improvement or pharmacology but by the Spirit, who opposes the flesh (Galatians 5:16–17). She ends with Jeremiah 2:13's broken cisterns and the promise of Matthew 5:6. A Christian may use these drugs or refuse them, as health dictates, under a doctor's care. What a Christian may never do is stop desiring God.
stories.counterpoint: Framing a metabolic disease chiefly through the language of vice risks loading moral weight onto patients whose weight owes much to genetics and environment, something Mantravadi acknowledges but does not fully resolve. And the scattered reports of flattened mood are anecdotes, not evidence that the drugs dull spiritual desire; the theological questions may run ahead of the science.
stories.why: For preaching and teaching, it recovers gluttony as Gregory and Aquinas understood it, a disorder of wanting, not a matter of body size, and gives a usable exegetical spine in Numbers 11, Deuteronomy 12 and Psalm 145. It equips pastors to speak to the one in eight adults on these drugs without either shaming or ignoring them, by pointing every appetite towards its proper end.
questions: Which of Gregory's five forms of gluttony are most invisible in your own life or church?
If a medicine can quiet a craving, what is left of the moral struggle, and what is not?
How would you preach Numbers 11 so that it addresses desire rather than diet?
